docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Serial Communications

These notes on serial data communications are intended to introduce some practical applications of the technology in the early part of a module in data networking. These notes are an introduction and are intended to let us share a basis of terminology and understanding.

It may seem anachronistic to be studying a technology that dates back to the earliest days of computing. However, this remains the technology we use every day. In these notes I'm going to focus on old fashioned Serial! In your own time, do a little reading with respect to USB. You will see that many of the principles are exactly the same, with a very different electrical interface.

docs.title: Fundamentals
docs.text:
Long, long ago, we had to come up with ways of data signalling. One of the first ideas was that of Morse code, a series of binary digits (dot and dash) which encoded letters and numbers. The unit of time duration for the message was based on the length of a dot.

  • A dash has the same time duration as three dots
  • Each dot or dash is separated by a time duration equal to one dot
  • Individual letters were spaced with a time duration of three dots
  • Words were spaced with a time duration of seven dots

There is no timing signal from side to side, the operator listens to the timing and gets it by ear. We call a link like this asynchronous.

Generally, the length of symbols was chosen based on letter frequency; the likelihood of being used in English. For example, the most common letter in the language (E) is a single dot, less common letters use up to four dot/dash combinations. They almost got it right, most analysts figure Morse code is about 90% efficient.

Fig 1. Asynchronous Serial.

We have a perfect example of asynchronous serial communications. Perhaps we could improve the accuracy if we send a timing signal. If we had a metronome sound going at exactly the frequency of transmission, it might be easier to figure out the timing.

Fig 2. Clock signal.

This would be synchronous serial communications.

docs.title: ASCII Encoding
docs.text:
In modern serial communications, we are more likely to use 8-bit ASCII coding. Although 7-bit ASCII exists, nothing has used it for a generation or more. 8-bit ASCII provides Latin characters, upper and lower case, numbers and many symbols.

Fig 3. Ascii Table.

This table was generated in EXCEL using the CHAR() command.

As an exercise, try to generate a copy of this table now for your own reference.

docs.title: RS232
docs.text:
With RS232, we can convert ASCII to an asynchronous signal.

To transmit the 8 bits of serial data, we need to know if the equipment is expecting the most significant bit (MSB) or least significant bit (LSB) first. For most of the protocols we will work with, its LSB first.

Fig 4. The letter A.

The letter A is 65 in base 10, 41 in base 16, or 0100 0001 in binary.

The waveform is discernible, but we could struggle to count the zeros in the middle. In real asynchronous communications, the letters arrive at random intervals, somehow, we need to know when a message starts.

The most basic serial protocol we use is RS232. When there is no signal, the line is high or “1”.

To signal the start of a character, a start bit of zero is inserted. If we know the speed of link, we know how much time should elapse from the start of the start bit to the middle of the next bit. At 9,600 bit/second the time between bits is 1.042 x 10-4 seconds. This tells us when to sample each bit position.

Fig 5. Start Bit.

Just to avoid confusion, the one in this case is negative and the zero is positive!

If the last bit of the signal was zero, we would need some way to distinguish the end of the symbol. This is a stop bit and the options are one or two.

Fig 6. Stop Bits.

The final option for a symbol is whether to put a parity check on it. The parity characteristic can be;

  • Even, the last data bit transmitted will be a logical 1 if the data transmitted had an even amount of 0 bits
  • Odd, the last data bit transmitted will be a logical 1 if the data transmitted had an odd amount of 0 bits
  • Mark, the last transmitted data bit will always be a logical 1
  • Space, the last transmitted data bit will always be a logical 0
  • None, no parity bit is transmitted

docs.title: Default Settings
docs.text:
Most RS232 ports of communications equipment are marked “9600-8-N-1” which means 9600 bits/second, 8 bits, no parity, one stop bit.

Equipment I have commissioned since 2020 has a default bit-rate of 115,200 bits/second.

docs.title: Voltage Levels
docs.text:
RS-232 uses bipolar voltage levels.

  • A positive voltage (+3VDC to +15VDC) for a logic zero
  • A negative voltage (-3VDC to -15VDC) for a logic one

Most electronics uses TTL levels where

  • 0V = logic zero
  • 5VDC = logic one

Some electronics uses 3.3VDC as the high voltage! Mixing these systems will result in permanent damage to the electroics. We need to use level shifter adapters to convert from one to the other.

docs.title: RS422 and 485
docs.text:
In previous notes, we saw that despite the simplicity and ubiquity of RS232. It does have some major drawbacks.

  • Its range is limited
  • Its bandwidth is limited and related to range
  • It is point to point, one duplex connection per link.

Other physical protocols have been developed to eliminate these issues and are commonly used in industrial communications. In data centers, we will find them in the automation of Power and Heating, Ventilation and Cooling/Air Conditioning (HVAC).

For example, RS422 can transmit to up to 10 receivers and can communicate at up to 10 Mb/s. It uses balanced, differential communications which provides much better noise immunity than RS232. RS422 can be used for long range point-to-point links, as a replacement for RS232. It should also be used where a single MASTER device will transmit data to (up to) ten SLAVE devices. If you examine a boat which is wired for traditional electronic instruments, you will see the use of a communications standard NMEA0183 and the physical standard RS422.

RS422 should not be used where bi-directional data is required between multiple devices; we use RS485 for this functionality. Process control systems have used this protocol for many years. 

Up to thirty-two RS485 transceivers can occupy a single bus and can communicate at up to 10 Mb/s. It uses balanced, differential communications which provides much better noise immunity than RS232. RS485 is used where multiple transceivers must communicate and each transceiver is part of a multi-drop network. Devices are daisy-chained together, and each device has a unique address. It can also be used in 4 wire mode, where a master device driver can connect to the receivers of all slave devices and the slave drivers are connected to the master receiver.

RS485 is used as the basis for many industrial data communications systems, including PROFIBUS. MODBUS based systems are also commonly implemented using RS485. Look up CANBUS, this is used in industry and in automotive vehicles.

Where an RS485 bus is greater than 1200m long, repeaters may be used to extend the bus.

I'm not gong to cover it here, but another option for long range communications is to use a 4-20mA current loop.

docs.title: Balanced v. Unbalanced
docs.text:
In RS232, each signal appears on a single line with reference to a signal ground. When noise is picked up on a single signal line, it also shows with respect to ground. Once the noise level exceeds +/-3V, it may appear as a bit and errors will occur. This is an unbalanced signal line and although it has the advantage of simplicity, it is very limited in its usage.

Fig 7. Unbalanced signal.

With balanced signals, two signal lines are dedicated per signal (A and B) and these lines carry opposite signals. When A is negative with respect to B, this is a binary one. When A is positive with respect to B, that is a binary zero.

Fig 8. Balanced signal.

When noise occurs, it shows with the same polarity on each line and can be cancelled. The signal shows as a differential value between the two signal lines and is much easier to detect.

docs.title: Voltage Levels
docs.text:
Voltage levels for RS485 are much smaller than those used for RS232.

  • +200mV DC to +6V DC is a logical zero
  • -200mV DC to -6V DC is a logical one

The diagram shows the levels for the A line with respect to B.

Fig 9. Voltage levels.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
In a RS485 system, both the transmit sides require 2 wires, a basic link will be 4 wires plus a reference earth. It is possible to bridge two wires of the driver and receiver such that the external wiring will work in 2 wire mode plus a reference earth. Be warned, some implementations on cheap interfaces are not isolated, I have fried computer equipment in the past!

Cheap boards are never cheap!

The additional cost of using screened cable is minimal, this is recommended. The screen is connected to earth at one side only. Typical cables are AWG24 or 0.5mm and there are a range of recommended cables. CAT5e STP may also be used, it is cheap and exceeds specifications.

To allow 32 devices on a bus to both receive and transmit, there are some special considerations. The receiver of each node will always be connected to the bus and listening. The transmitter or driver can be transmitting a one, or a zero, or can be disabled from transmitting to the bus. It must be disabled when not in use, otherwise it would hold the bus at a one (idle state). As it can be in any one of three states, it is referred to as a tri-state device. Each driver has an enable line which must be active for the driver to connect to the bus. Many systems use the standard control signal RTS for this function. Where multiple systems share such a bus, each device must have a unique ID. We refer to this as a multi-drop bus. Once there are multiple nodes on a bus, the communications protocol must govern who speaks. This system will be half-duplex and a protocol like MODBUS will arbitrate who speaks.

Simplex communications occur when a single device transmits and is received by a receiver.

Duplex communications implies two separate signal paths, where each device can transmit and receive at the same time

docs.title: Terminators
docs.text:
Every wire has physical properties which relate to its construction. One of these properties is called the characteristic impedance, the apparent impedance of the line to an AC signal. For good clean signal transmission, it is usually required to terminate a signal line at either end. The standards for RS485 specify a 120Ω resistor.

Terminators can have disadvantages; they do add to the load that the node’s driver will experience.

If the propagation delay on the line is less than one bit long, terminators are not necessary. For low speeds (<=38.4kb/s) termination is normally not required.

Placement of terminators may be complex but normally they will be assigned at the end of a bus, two per bus.

Some vendors recommend the use of AC terminators, where a resistor and a capacitor are used so that the line is terminated but does not cause a DC loading.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
One of the issues we have when connecting two devices across a copper wire, it that the ground potential on the two sides may be different. This may cause there to be a common mode voltage difference between the two sides which may damage the equipment. The reason we have a reference earth connection is to tie all nodes to a common ground. The RS485 standard specifies this should not exceed -7VDC – +12VDC.

Circumstances may exist when very large voltages are experienced on the nodes. In many cases, signals are optically isolated by optocouplers to prevent such high voltages doing damage. Where transients occur, these may be exceptionally high voltage and frequency. Protection for these include devices which break down under such circumstances. These are called shunts and there are a family of such devices.

docs.title: Experimentation
docs.text:
The Raspberry PI (RPi) is a very handy tool for experimenting with serial communications, I use a range of interface HATS to do development work with serial protocols.

RS232 is built-in, one usable port on early board. Although there are 6 serial ports on a RPi 4, they are frustratingly difficult to use as they overlap with other functions.

The other protocols mentioned in this paper require some special boards.

Fig 10. RPi Interfaces.

In the photograph (Fig 10), the board on the left is a high-quality serial board, which I use for RS422 marine telemetry and NMEA0183. One version of that board supports the more modern CANBUS-like standard NMEA2000.

The board on the right is an inexpensive RS485 interface.

docs.title: Virtualised Experimentation
docs.text:
I do not want you to test this, there is only so much we can pack into any module!

When I'm doing experimentation work, I can do so in a virtualized environment. If I'm working on a domain specific language (DSL) used for encoding information, I will first set up a simple Linux VM to generate the DSL, a simulator. Using a technology like VMware workstation, I can configure serial links between two devices. On the second VM, I can then create a parser for the DSL. It sounds complicated, but this is a standard methodology.

To start, I install pyserial.

pip install pyserial

I asked ChatGPT to generate a simple serial chat program for me. it uses multithreading so that send and recieve can happen simultaneously.

import serial
import threading


# Set the corrent port device!
PORT = "/dev/ttyS0" 
BAUDRATE = 9600

ser = serial.Serial(PORT, BAUDRATE, timeout=1)

def receive():
    # Continuously read incoming messages
    while True:
        try:
            data = ser.readline().decode("utf-8").strip()
            if data:
                print(f"\nPeer: {data}")
        except Exception:
            break

# Start receiver thread
threading.Thread(target=receive, daemon=True).start()

print("Serial chat started. Type messages and press Enter.\n")

# Main send loop
while True:
    try:
        msg = input("You: ")
        ser.write((msg + "\n").encode("utf-8"))
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("\nExiting chat.")
        break

ser.close()

Once the source and parser appear to be working, they are saved to a git repo and then I can comfortably copy them down to physical hardware for the next stage of testing using a git clone. Up to now, I have only tested this as a simulator. At this point I begin hooking up to a reference source, a piece of real equipment to test against.
